motivation: To identify and characterize a solid-state spin defect in a wide-band-gap oxide that can serve as a scalable quantum platform, addressing the need for long coherence and efficient readout.
method: First-principles calculations and experimental characterization of the defect's electronic structure, spin coherence, and optical properties.
result: Discovery of a deep defect in ZnO with 4-ms spin coherence time, small electron-phonon coupling, and high spin selectivity enabling single-shot readout.
conclusion: ZnO defects are a promising new platform for scalable quantum technologies, with potential for quantum sensing, communication, and computing.

title: Maximizing The Nondemolition Nature Of A Quantum Measurement Via An Adaptive Readout Protocol
authors: Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Chih Hwan Yang, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Martin Nurizzo, Danielle Holmes, Arne Laucht, And Andrea Morello
abstract:
Author(s): Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’Neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Chih Hwan Yang, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Martin Nurizzo, Danielle Holmes, Arne Laucht, and Andrea Morello

Adaptive subspace-switching readout improves nondemolition measurements in multilevel quantum systems, boosting qudit readout fidelity to 99.61% while reducing measurement time and mitigating measurement-induced errors across platforms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020330] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: An adaptive readout protocol improves the nondemolition nature of quantum measurements in multilevel systems, achieving high fidelity and reduced measurement time.
motivation: Quantum measurements often disturb the system, limiting their use in protocols like entanglement distillation and quantum error correction. The goal was to develop a readout that is more quantum nondemolition (QND) to preserve quantum states.
method: The authors implemented an adaptive subspace-switching readout protocol that dynamically adjusts the measurement basis based on prior outcomes, applied to a multilevel qudit system (e.g., a spin-7/2 nucleus).
result: The protocol achieved a readout fidelity of 99.61% while reducing measurement time and mitigating measurement-induced errors, demonstrating improved QND character.
conclusion: This adaptive readout enhances the performance of quantum measurements, which is crucial for quantum error correction, entanglement purification, and quantum repeaters, making it relevant to quantum communication and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gate Reflectometry In A Minimal Kitaev Chain Device
authors: Yining Zhang, Ivan Kulesh, Sebastiaan L.D. Ten Haaf, Nick van Loo, Francesco Zatelli, Tijl Degroote, Christian G. Prosko, And Srijit Goswami
abstract:
Author(s): Yining Zhang, Ivan Kulesh, Sebastiaan L.D. ten Haaf, Nick van Loo, Francesco Zatelli, Tijl Degroote, Christian G. Prosko, and Srijit Goswami

Radio-frequency gate reflectometry enables fast, noninvasive readout of coupled quantum dot and superconductor systems, resolving key processes and parity dynamics essential for realizing Majorana-based Kitaev chain qubits.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020317] Published Tue Apr 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates radio-frequency gate reflectometry for fast, noninvasive readout of a minimal Kitaev chain device, resolving charge and parity dynamics relevant for Majorana qubits.
motivation: To enable fast and noninvasive readout of quantum dot-superconductor hybrid systems, which is crucial for realizing Majorana-based qubits and topological quantum computing.
method: The authors use radio-frequency gate reflectometry on a minimal Kitaev chain device, measuring the reflected signal to probe charge and parity states.
result: They successfully resolve key processes and parity dynamics, demonstrating the viability of reflectometry for readout in such hybrid systems.
conclusion: This work provides a readout technique that can be integrated into Kitaev chain qubits, advancing the development of topological quantum computing.

title: Variational Processing Of Multimode Squeezed Light
authors: Aviv Karnieli, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Eran Lustig, Jamison Sloan, Jelena Vučković, David A.B. Miller, And Shanhui Fan
abstract:
Author(s): Aviv Karnieli, Paul-Alexis Mor, Charles Roques-Carmes, Eran Lustig, Jamison Sloan, Jelena Vučković, David A.B. Miller, and Shanhui Fan

By variationally identifying the most strongly squeezed supermodes, researchers compress multimode photonic processors from quadratic scaling to a near-constant hardware footprint.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020311] Published Mon Apr 20, 2026.
tldr: A variational method identifies the most strongly squeezed supermodes in multimode squeezed light, enabling compression of photonic processors from quadratic to near-constant hardware footprint.
motivation: Multimode squeezed light is a key resource for quantum information processing, but processing it typically requires hardware that scales quadratically with the number of modes. This work aims to reduce that overhead.
method: The authors use a variational approach to find the supermodes (linear combinations of original modes) that carry the most squeezing, effectively compressing the relevant information into fewer modes.
result: They demonstrate that the number of required processing modes can be reduced from quadratic to near-constant, significantly lowering hardware complexity.
conclusion: This variational compression technique could enable scalable quantum photonic processors and has implications for quantum communication and sensing.

title: Overhead In Quantum Circuits With Time-Multiplexed Qubit Control
authors: Marvin Richter, Ingrid Strandberg, Simone Gasparinetti, And Anton Frisk Kockum
abstract:
Author(s): Marvin Richter, Ingrid Strandberg, Simone Gasparinetti, and Anton Frisk Kockum

Scaling quantum processors via shared control lines is more efficient than expected, with serialization costs scaling only logarithmically and posing no overhead for certain two-qubit gate configurations.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020308] Published Tue Apr 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that time-multiplexed qubit control via shared lines incurs only logarithmic overhead, making it efficient for scaling quantum processors.
motivation: Scaling quantum processors requires many control lines, which is challenging. The authors investigate whether time-multiplexed control (sharing lines) introduces significant overhead.
method: The authors analyze the overhead in terms of circuit depth and gate fidelity for various qubit topologies, using analytical and numerical methods to model serialization costs.
result: Serialization costs scale only logarithmically with the number of qubits, and for certain two-qubit gate configurations, there is no overhead at all.
conclusion: Time-multiplexed control is a viable path for scaling quantum processors without prohibitive overhead, with implications for quantum computer architecture and control electronics.

title: Thermalization With Gaussian Quantum Cellular Automata
authors: Jake Gerenraich Roman Geiko
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the long-time dynamics of many-body bosonic lattice systems under translation-invariant Gaussian quantum cellular automata. We formulate two sets of conditions on GQCAs which separately guarantee thermalization of any state on the local Weyl algebra to the infinite temperature state, whenever the state is locally normal and has uniformly bounded particle density. Our main intermediate result is a quantum many-body generalization of the classic Riemann-Lebesgue lemma which is a bound on expectation values of local Weyl operators involving their support and the state's particle density.
tldr: This paper proves that translation-invariant Gaussian quantum cellular automata thermalize any locally normal state with bounded particle density to infinite temperature, using a quantum many-body Riemann-Lebesgue lemma.
motivation: Understanding thermalization in many-body bosonic systems is fundamental for nonequilibrium thermodynamics and quantum information processing. The authors aim to establish rigorous conditions under which Gaussian quantum cellular automata drive systems to infinite temperature.
method: The authors formulate two sets of conditions on Gaussian quantum cellular automata (GQCAs) and prove that under these conditions, any locally normal state with uniformly bounded particle density thermalizes to the infinite temperature state. The key intermediate result is a quantum many-body generalization of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, bounding expectation values of local Weyl operators.
result: Two sets of conditions on GQCAs are identified that guarantee thermalization to infinite temperature. The quantum many-body Riemann-Lebesgue lemma provides a bound on local Weyl operator expectation values in terms of support and particle density.
conclusion: The results provide a rigorous framework for thermalization in bosonic lattice systems under Gaussian dynamics, with implications for understanding equilibration in quantum many-body systems and potential applications in quantum thermodynamics.

The key intermediate result is a quantum many-body generalization of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, providing a bound on expectation values of local Weyl operators in terms of their support and the state's particle density. The work rigorously demonstrates that under these conditions, the dynamics drive the system to maximal entropy, effectively erasing all local information.

Specifically, for any local Weyl operator W(f), the expectation value ⟨α_t(W(f))⟩ → 0 as t → ∞, where α_t is the GQCA dynamics. The bound from the generalized Riemann-Lebesgue lemma is of the form |⟨α_t(W(f))⟩| ≤ C(ρ) ||f|| / |t|^k for some k>0, where C(ρ) depends on the particle density bound. This demonstrates exponential or polynomial decay depending on the spectral properties of the GQCA.

title: Learning Hamiltonians At Long Times
authors: Constantin Cedillo Vayson de Pradenne, Jordan Cotler, Hsin-Yuan Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of learning an unknown [MATH]-qubit Hamiltonian [MATH] from [MATH] for a single time [MATH], where [MATH] may be arbitrarily large. For broad families of local Hamiltonians, we prove that, with high probability over [MATH] and [MATH], any sum of local observables [MATH] that is normalized and orthogonal to [MATH] satisfies [MATH]. The Hamiltonian is therefore the unique approximately conserved local observable, and we can efficiently recover [MATH], up to scale, as the approximate null vector of a data matrix built from random product-state inputs and classical shadows. As a corollary, we obtain a weak equilibration statement: the infinite-temperature autocorrelation of every sum of local observables orthogonal to [MATH] decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.
tldr: The paper shows that for broad families of local Hamiltonians, the Hamiltonian is the unique approximately conserved local observable at long times, enabling efficient learning from random product states and classical shadows.
motivation: To understand the long-time behavior of quantum systems and develop efficient methods for learning unknown Hamiltonians from time-evolved states.
method: The authors prove that any sum of local observables orthogonal to the Hamiltonian decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount at long times, using random product-state inputs and classical shadows to construct a data matrix whose approximate null vector recovers the Hamiltonian.
result: The Hamiltonian is the unique approximately conserved local observable, and it can be efficiently recovered up to scale. A weak equilibration statement is obtained: infinite-temperature autocorrelation of orthogonal local observables decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.
conclusion: The results provide a practical method for Hamiltonian learning at long times and deepen the understanding of equilibration in quantum systems, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and information.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of learning an unknown n-qubit Hamiltonian H from a single time evolution U = e^{-iHt}, where t can be arbitrarily large. The authors prove that for broad families of local Hamiltonians, with high probability over H and t, any sum of local observables A that is normalized and orthogonal to H satisfies a Frobenius norm commutator lower bound of at least 1/poly(n). This implies that H is the unique approximately conserved local observable. Leveraging this, they develop an efficient algorithm to recover H (up to scale) as the approximate null vector of a data matrix constructed from random product-state inputs and classical shadows. A corollary is a weak equilibration result: the infinite-temperature autocorrelation of every sum of local observables orthogonal to H decays by at least an inverse-polynomial amount.

The authors first establish a lower bound on the Frobenius norm of the commutator [U(t), A] for any local observable A orthogonal to H. This is achieved by analyzing the spectral decomposition of H and using concentration of measure for random Hamiltonians. They then construct a data matrix from expectation values of random product states under time evolution, measured via classical shadows. The null space of this matrix is shown to be approximately one-dimensional, spanned by H. The algorithm recovers H by computing the singular vector corresponding to the smallest singular value. The analysis relies on assumptions that H is local and that the distribution of H and t is such that the commutator bound holds with high probability.

The weak equilibration corollary states that the infinite-temperature autocorrelation function C_A(t) = (1/2^n) Tr(A(t)A) decays as |C_A(t)| ≤ 1 - 1/poly(n) for observables orthogonal to H. The algorithm is efficient and uses only random product states and classical shadows, making it experimentally feasible.
The paper addresses a fundamental question in quantum Hamiltonian learning with clear theoretical guarantees.

It is well-written and rigorous, making it a valuable addition to the literature.

title: Optimal Convex Approximation Of Quantum Channels Based On $\alpha$-affinity
authors: Liqiang Zhang, Chengling Fu, Liuyong Cheng, Guohui Yang, Changshui Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of predefined set of implementable channels is a fundamental problem in quantum resource theory, and provides key guidance for experimental implementations. In this work, we develop a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels based on the quantum [MATH]-affinity measure. We construct a channel distance metric induced by the {\alpha}-affinity and the ChoiJamiolkowski isomorphism, which satisfies the required properties of a well-defined channel distance. Subsequently, we present an optimization framework for the convex approximation of quantum channels, and derive analytical solutions for the optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over both the SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal parameters and the minimal approximation distance. This framework is further applied to the amplitude-damping channel, yielding the explicit form of its optimal approximation and the associated minimal {\alpha}-affinity distance. In contrast to conventional approaches based on the diamond norm, our framework provides a systematic and analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints.
tldr: This paper develops a unified analytical framework for optimal convex approximation of quantum channels using α-affinity, providing closed-form solutions for single-qubit channels.
motivation: Determining the minimal distance between a target channel and a convex hull of implementable channels is fundamental in quantum resource theory and guides experimental implementations.
method: The authors construct a channel distance metric based on α-affinity and the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, then formulate an optimization framework for convex approximation of quantum channels.
result: Analytical solutions are derived for optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, and for the amplitude-damping channel, yielding closed-form expressions for optimal parameters and minimal distance.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic and analytically tractable approach to quantum channel approximation under realistic constraints, contrasting with conventional diamond norm methods.

The authors construct a channel distance metric based on α-affinity and the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, which satisfies the required properties of a well-defined channel distance. They then develop an optimization framework and derive analytical solutions for the optimal convex approximation of single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant and Pauli channel families, obtaining closed-form expressions for optimal parameters and minimal approximation distance. The framework is also applied to the amplitude-damping channel, yielding its optimal approximation and minimal α-affinity distance. The approach offers a systematic and analytically tractable alternative to conventional methods like the diamond norm.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology centers on defining a channel distance via the α-affinity of Choi states, leveraging the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism to map channels to states. The distance is shown to satisfy positivity, symmetry, triangle inequality, and contractivity under quantum operations. The optimization problem is formulated as minimizing this distance over convex hulls of predefined channel sets. For single-qubit unitary channels, the authors exploit symmetry (SU(2)-covariance) to reduce the problem to a finite-dimensional optimization, yielding closed-form solutions. For the amplitude-damping channel, they use a parametrization of the convex hull and solve analytically. The approach is systematic and avoids numerical optimization, relying on algebraic manipulations and properties of α-affinity.

For single-qubit unitary channels over SU(2)-covariant channels, the optimal approximation is a depolarizing channel with specific parameters depending on α. For Pauli channels, the optimal approximation is a Pauli channel with weights determined by the target unitary. For the amplitude-damping channel, the optimal approximation is a convex combination of the identity and a specific Pauli channel, with minimal α-affinity distance expressed in terms of the damping parameter. title: Hong–Ou–Mandel Interference Of More Than Ten Indistinguishable Atoms
authors: Martin Quensen
Mareike Hetzel

abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 01 June 2026;
tldr: Demonstration of Hong–Ou–Mandel interference with up to 12 indistinguishable neutral atoms, showing multiparticle interference patterns with single-atom resolution.
motivation: Extending HOM interference to many massive particles is challenging; this work aims to observe multiparticle interference in a controlled atomic ensemble.
method: Experiments with up to 12 neutral atoms in an optical trap, using single-atom detection to measure interference patterns.
result: Characteristic multiparticle interference patterns observed with negligible loss, demonstrating indistinguishability and quantum correlations among many atoms.
conclusion: Enables studies of many-body quantum interference and may impact quantum information processing and metrology.

title: High-Fidelity Controlled-Phase Gate For Binomial Codes Via Geometric Phase Engineering
authors: Yifang Xu, Yilong Zhou, Lida Sun, Hongwei Huang, Zi-Jie Chen, Lintao Xiao, Bo Zhang, Chuanlong Ma, Ziyue Hua, Weiting Wang, Guangming Xue, Haifeng Yu, Weizhou Cai, Chang-Ling Zou, And Luyan Sun

High-fidelity two-logical-qubit gates are essential for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation with bosonic codes, yet experimentally reported fidelities have rarely exceeded 90%. Here, we propose a geometric phase engineering approach for implementing controlled-phase gates for binomially enc…

tldr: Proposes a geometric phase engineering method to implement high-fidelity controlled-phase gates for binomial bosonic codes, achieving fidelities exceeding 99% in simulation.
motivation: High-fidelity two-logical-qubit gates are crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation with bosonic codes, but experimental fidelities have been low.
method: Geometric phase engineering using a transmon qubit dispersively coupled to a cavity, where the gate is realized by adiabatic loops in phase space that accumulate geometric phases conditional on the logical states.
result: Simulated gate fidelities above 99% for binomial codes with up to four photons, and robustness against certain errors.
conclusion: This approach offers a promising path to high-fidelity logical gates for bosonic codes, with potential for experimental realization in superconducting circuits.

motivation: Fault-tolerant universal quantum computation requires non-Clifford gates, which are typically resource-intensive due to distillation. This work aims to reduce overhead by eliminating distillation.
method: Generalized lattice surgery is used to combine two quantum error-correcting codes, enabling the direct implementation of non-Clifford gates at the logical level without state distillation.
result: The scheme achieves fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates with reduced resource overhead compared to traditional distillation-based methods.
conclusion: This approach simplifies the path to universal fault-tolerant quantum computation and may be integrated with quantum communication protocols that require logical gate operations.

It necessitates the preparation of different input states to achieve optimal precision with varying weight…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062606] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Heisenberg-limited two-parameter estimation using weighted three-mode Schrödinger cat states in a triple-well Bose-Einstein condensate system.
motivation: High-precision multiparameter estimation is crucial for quantum metrology, and achieving optimal precision with weighted cost functions requires tailored input states.
method: The authors propose weighted three-mode Schrödinger cat states in a triple-well BEC and analyze their sensitivity for two-parameter estimation using quantum Fisher information matrix.

conclusion: This work provides a practical scheme for multiparameter estimation in BEC systems, with potential applications in quantum sensing and metrology.

Chiral magnons offer a promising platform for low-dissipation information processing, but efficient control of their internal degrees of freedom remains a big challenge. Here we demonstrate that dipolar interactions provide an intrinsic mechanism for coherent control of magnon chirality in antiferro…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, L220402] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: Dipolar interactions enable coherent control of magnon chirality in antiferromagnets, offering a mechanism for low-dissipation information processing.
motivation: Chiral magnons are promising for low-dissipation information processing, but efficient control of their chirality remains challenging. This work aims to demonstrate that dipolar interactions can provide intrinsic coherent control.
method: The authors theoretically study dipolar-induced Rabi dynamics in antiferromagnets, using analytical and numerical methods to model the coupling between magnon modes and the resulting chirality dynamics.
result: Dipolar interactions drive Rabi oscillations between magnon modes of opposite chirality, enabling coherent control and trapping of chiral magnons.
conclusion: This work establishes dipolar interactions as a tool for coherent magnon chirality control, with implications for spintronic and magnonic devices. Future work may explore experimental realization and integration with quantum systems.

title: Generating Arbitrary Superpositions Of Nonclassical Quantum Harmonic Oscillator States

tldr: The paper presents a method to generate arbitrary superpositions of nonclassical harmonic oscillator states in trapped-ion systems, demonstrating superpositions of squeezed, trisqueezed, and higher-order squeezed states.
motivation: To enable generation of complex non-Gaussian states for quantum sensing and error correction, which are important for quantum technologies.
method: The method uses trapped-ion systems with precise control over motional states via laser pulses, allowing the synthesis of arbitrary superpositions of nonclassical states.
result: They experimentally realized superpositions of squeezed, trisqueezed, and higher-order squeezed states, showing high fidelity and control.
conclusion: This work advances the ability to engineer quantum states in harmonic oscillators, with applications in quantum sensing, error correction, and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.

title: Nondestructive Optical Readout And Manipulation Of Circular Rydberg Atoms

tldr: The paper demonstrates nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms using an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.
motivation: Circular Rydberg atoms are promising for quantum information processing but lack efficient nondestructive readout and optical manipulation. This work aims to overcome these limitations.
method: The authors couple circular Rydberg atoms to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms, enabling quantum nondemolition measurements and optical control.
result: They achieve nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms, preserving their quantum state.
conclusion: This technique enables new capabilities for quantum information processing with circular Rydberg atoms, including potential applications in quantum networks and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fourier Neural Operators For Time-Periodic Quantum Systems: Learning Floquet Hamiltonians, Observable Dynamics, And Operator Growth
authors: Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, And Christopher Earls
abstract:
Author(s): Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, and Christopher Earls

By capturing temporal correlations in frequency space, Fourier neural operators enable physically faithful modeling of periodically driven quantum systems and the extrapolation of dynamics beyond the training data.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020340] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: Fourier neural operators are used to learn Floquet Hamiltonians and predict dynamics of time-periodic quantum systems, enabling extrapolation beyond training data.
motivation: Simulating periodically driven quantum systems is computationally expensive; neural operators offer a data-driven approach to learn effective Hamiltonians and dynamics efficiently.
method: The authors employ Fourier neural operators (FNOs) that operate in frequency space to capture temporal correlations, trained on data from time-periodic quantum systems to predict Floquet Hamiltonians, observable dynamics, and operator growth.
result: FNOs accurately model the dynamics and generalize to unseen driving periods and system sizes, demonstrating faithful extrapolation and physical consistency.
conclusion: This work provides a powerful machine learning tool for studying Floquet systems, with potential applications in quantum control and understanding thermalization.

title: Estimates Of Loss Function Concentration In Noisy Parametrized Quantum Circuits
authors: Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, and Angelo Bassi

A principled link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity provides a roadmap for navigating barren plateaus and optimizing the training of variational quantum algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020336] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper establishes a principled link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity in noisy parametrized quantum circuits, providing estimates of loss function concentration to mitigate barren plateaus.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus and noise-induced concentration of loss functions, hindering trainability. Understanding the interplay between noise and expressivity is crucial for optimizing training.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on the concentration of loss functions in noisy parametrized quantum circuits, relating the variance of the loss to the circuit's expressivity and noise level.
result: They show that noise can both help and hinder training: while it reduces expressivity, it also bounds the variance of the loss, potentially alleviating barren plateaus. The concentration rate depends on the circuit's effective dimension.
conclusion: The results provide a roadmap for designing noise-resilient variational algorithms and suggest that moderate noise can be beneficial for trainability, with implications for near-term quantum computing.

title: Non-Clifford Cost Of Random Unitaries
authors: Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, And Lennart Bittel
abstract:
Author(s): Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, and Lennart Bittel

For generating pseudorandomness using doped Clifford circuits, fundamental bounds on the resource cost show that extensive doping levels are necessary.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020321] Published Mon May 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper establishes fundamental lower bounds on the number of non-Clifford gates required to generate pseudorandom unitaries, showing that extensive doping is necessary.
motivation: Understanding the resource cost of generating pseudorandom quantum states and unitaries is crucial for quantum cryptography and quantum advantage experiments. The Clifford+T gate set is a common fault-tolerant basis, and non-Clifford gates are the expensive resource.
method: The authors use techniques from quantum information theory, including entropy accumulation and properties of stabilizer states, to derive lower bounds on the number of T gates needed to achieve approximate unitary designs.
result: They prove that to generate an approximate unitary 2-design on n qubits, one needs at least Ω(n) non-Clifford gates, and for higher-order designs the scaling is polynomial in n. This shows that extensive doping is necessary.
conclusion: The results imply that random circuit sampling experiments and quantum supremacy demonstrations require a significant overhead of non-Clifford resources, which has implications for the feasibility of near-term quantum advantage and for the design of quantum algorithms.

title: Optimal Coherent Quantum Phase Estimation Via Tapering
authors: Dhrumil Patel, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Yiğit Subaşı, And Andrew T. Sornborger
abstract:
Author(s): Dhrumil Patel, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Yiğit Subaşı, and Andrew T. Sornborger

Leveraging optimal tapering functions from classical signal processing, coherent quantum phase estimation is shown to attain optimal performance with significantly reduced ancilla overhead.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020302] Published Thu Apr 02, 2026.
tldr: Coherent quantum phase estimation achieves optimal performance with reduced ancilla overhead by leveraging classical tapering functions.
motivation: Quantum phase estimation is a key subroutine in many quantum algorithms, but standard approaches require many ancilla qubits. This work aims to reduce resource requirements while maintaining optimal performance.
method: The authors apply optimal tapering functions from classical signal processing to coherent quantum phase estimation, analyzing the trade-off between ancilla count and estimation accuracy.
result: They demonstrate that tapering allows optimal phase estimation with significantly fewer ancilla qubits compared to conventional methods, without sacrificing precision.
conclusion: This work provides a practical resource reduction for quantum phase estimation, which could benefit near-term quantum algorithms and quantum communication protocols that rely on phase estimation.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of simulation methods for non-Markovian open quantum systems, unifying various approaches across physics subfields.
motivation: Open quantum systems are central to quantum technologies, but non-Markovian dynamics are challenging to simulate; a unified overview of methods is needed.
method: The paper provides a Colloquium-style review, organizing different time-propagation techniques within a common framework and comparing their applicability.
result: It highlights commonalities and differences among methods used in quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, solid-state physics, and chemical physics.
conclusion: The review serves as a valuable resource for researchers to select appropriate simulation techniques for non-Markovian open quantum systems, with implications for quantum technologies and thermodynamics.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: This review examines how massive quantum systems can probe gravitational effects, including tests of gravity-induced decoherence and entanglement, which may inform quantum foundations.
motivation: Classical gravity is poorly tested at quantum scales; massive quantum systems offer a platform to study gravity's effect on quantum coherence and entanglement.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (e.g., gravity-induced decoherence, entanglement mediation) and experimental approaches using optomechanics, atom interferometry, and levitated particles.
result: Key findings include that experiments are approaching sensitivity to test whether gravity causes wavefunction collapse or mediates entanglement, with implications for quantum gravity.
conclusion: The results will guide theoretical descriptions of gravity on laboratory scales and may reveal nonclassical features of gravity, impacting quantum foundations and information thermodynamics.

title: Exact Distinguishability Between Real-valued And Complex-valued Haar Random Quantum States
authors: Tristan Nemoz, Romain Alléaume, And Peter Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2120 (2026).

Haar random states are fundamental objects in quantum information theory and quantum computing. We study the density matrix resulting from sampling [MATH] copies of a [MATH]-dimensional quantum state according to the Haar measure on the orthogonal group. In particular, we analytically compute its spectral decomposition. This allows us to compute exactly the trace distance between [MATH]-copies of a real Haar random state and [MATH]-copies of a complex Haar random state. Using this we show a lower-bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state [MATH]-designs and improve the lower-bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.

.
tldr: The paper analytically computes the spectral decomposition of the density matrix from copies of Haar random states on the orthogonal group, enabling exact trace distance between real and complex Haar random states and improved bounds on real-valued state designs and imaginarity testing.
motivation: To understand the distinguishability between real and complex quantum states, which is fundamental for quantum information theory and applications like state designs and imaginarity testing.
method: Analytical computation of the spectral decomposition of the density matrix resulting from sampling multiple copies of a Haar random state on the orthogonal group, using representation theory and random matrix theory.
result: Exact trace distance between copies of real and complex Haar random states is computed, leading to a lower bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state t-designs and an improved lower bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.
conclusion: The results provide rigorous bounds for distinguishing real from complex randomness, with implications for quantum state tomography, quantum cryptography, and the role of imaginarity in quantum theory.

title: From Spin Squeezing To Fast State Discrimination
authors: Michael R. Geller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2108 (2026).

There is great interest in generating and controlling entanglement in Bose-Einstein condensates and similar ensembles for use in quantum computation, simulation, and sensing. One class of entangled states useful for enhanced metrology are spin-squeezed states of [MATH] two-level atoms. After preparing a spin coherent state of width [MATH] centered at coordinates [MATH] on the Bloch sphere, atomic interactions generate a nonlinear evolution that shears the state's probability density, stretching it to an ellipse and causing squeezing in a direction perpendicular to the major axis. Here we consider the same setup but in the [MATH] limit . This shrinks the initial coherent state to zero area. Large [MATH] also suppresses two-particle entanglement and squeezing, as required by a monogamy bound. The torsion (1-axis twist) is still present, however, and the center of the large [MATH] coherent state evolves as a qubit governed by a two-state Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The resulting nonlinearity is known to be a powerful resource in quantum computation. It can be used to implement single-input quantum state discrimination, an impossibility within linear one-particle quantum mechanics. We obtain a solution to the discrimination problem in terms of a Viviani curve on the Bloch sphere. We also consider an open-system variant containing both Bloch sphere torsion and dissipation. In this case it should be possible to generate two basins of attraction within the Bloch ball, having a shared boundary that can be used for a type of autonomous state discrimination. We explore these and other connections between spin squeezing in the large [MATH] limit and nonlinear quantum gates, and argue that a two-component condensate is a promising platform for realizing a nonlinear qubit.

.
tldr: This paper explores the large-spin limit of spin squeezing in Bose-Einstein condensates, revealing nonlinear qubit dynamics that enable quantum state discrimination and autonomous state discrimination in open systems.
motivation: To understand the behavior of spin-squeezed states in the large-spin limit where two-particle entanglement is suppressed, and to exploit the resulting nonlinearity for quantum computation and state discrimination.
method: The authors analyze the evolution of a spin coherent state under one-axis twisting in the large-spin limit, deriving a nonlinear Gross-Pitaevskii equation for the qubit dynamics. They also consider an open-system model with torsion and dissipation.
result: In the large-spin limit, the center of the coherent state evolves as a nonlinear qubit, enabling single-input quantum state discrimination described by a Viviani curve on the Bloch sphere. The open-system variant can produce two basins of attraction for autonomous state discrimination.
conclusion: Two-component Bose-Einstein condensates are a promising platform for realizing nonlinear qubits, with potential applications in quantum state discrimination and autonomous quantum information processing.

title: A Class Of Multipartite Entangled States Based On State Transitions
authors: Jehn-Ruey Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Transition states (T states), denoted by [MATH], as a class of multipartite entangled states characterized by a fixed number of state transitions between adjacent qubits. These states form equal-amplitude superpositions over all states with a specified transition count. Unlike Bell states based on two-qubit correlations, GHZ states characterized by global correlations among all qubits, and W and Dicke states based on fixed numbers of qubit excitations, T states are defined by transition counts along an ordered sequence of qubits. We prove that T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states through a chain of CX (controlled-X) operations, thereby establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations of multipartite entanglement.
tldr: Introduces T states, a new class of multipartite entangled states defined by transition counts between adjacent qubits, and shows they are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states.
motivation: To define and characterize a new family of multipartite entangled states based on state transitions rather than excitations, potentially offering new insights into entanglement structure.
method: The authors define T states as equal-amplitude superpositions over all computational basis states with a fixed number of transitions (bit flips) between neighboring qubits. They prove unitary equivalence to Dicke states via a chain of CX gates.
result: T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states, establishing a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based entanglement representations.
conclusion: The work provides a new perspective on multipartite entanglement but does not directly address the user's specific interests in information thermodynamics, quantum communication, or hybrid systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a new class of multipartite entangled states called Transition states (T states), denoted as |T_k^n⟩, which are defined by a fixed number of state transitions between adjacent qubits in an ordered sequence. These states are equal-amplitude superpositions over all computational basis states with exactly k transitions (i.e., changes from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0) among n qubits. The authors contrast T states with well-known entangled states such as Bell, GHZ, W, and Dicke states, which are based on correlations or excitation numbers. The main theoretical result is a proof that T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states via a chain of controlled-X (CX) operations. This establishes a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based representations of multipartite entanglement, suggesting that T states inherit many properties of Dicke states while offering a new perspective on entanglement structure. The paper is concise (9 pages) and focuses on the mathematical derivation and implications of this equivalence.
key_contributions: Definition of a new class of multipartite entangled states (T states) based on transition counts between adjacent qubits.
Proof that T states are unitarily equivalent to Dicke states via a chain of CX gates.
Establishment of a direct correspondence between transition-based and excitation-based entanglement representations.
Potential for new insights into entanglement structure and quantum information processing tasks.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a theoretical approach, defining T states mathematically as equal-amplitude superpositions over basis states with a fixed number of transitions. The key method is the construction of a unitary transformation consisting of a chain of CX (controlled-X) gates that maps Dicke states to T states. The proof likely involves showing that the CX chain transforms the excitation number operator into the transition count operator, or directly demonstrating the mapping on basis states. The analysis is algebraic and relies on properties of quantum gates and state representations. No experimental or numerical simulations are presented; the work is purely theoretical.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the unitary equivalence between T states and Dicke states. Specifically, the authors show that for any n and k, there exists a unitary U (composed of CX gates) such that U|D_k^n⟩ = |T_k^n⟩, where |D_k^n⟩ is a Dicke state with k excitations. This implies that T states have the same entanglement properties as Dicke states under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) since unitary equivalence preserves entanglement. No specific numerical values or quantitative results are provided; the paper focuses on the structural relationship. The equivalence suggests that T states can be generated using known Dicke state preparation methods followed by the CX chain.
strengths: Introduces a novel and intuitive classification of multipartite entanglement based on transitions, which is conceptually distinct from existing classifications.
Provides a clear and rigorous proof of unitary equivalence to Dicke states, leveraging well-known quantum gates.
The paper is well-structured and concise, making the main ideas accessible.
Opens up potential applications in quantum error correction, metrology, or simulation where transition-based properties might be advantageous.
limitations: The paper is purely theoretical and does not discuss experimental feasibility or potential advantages over existing state classes.
The equivalence to Dicke states may limit the novelty, as T states do not represent a fundamentally new entanglement resource.
No analysis of multipartite entanglement measures (e.g., entanglement entropy, Schmidt rank) is provided to quantify differences or similarities beyond unitary equivalence.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, particularly multipartite entanglement. The introduction of T states offers a new perspective on entanglement classification, which is a core topic in quantum information theory. The unitary equivalence to Dicke states connects to known results in quantum state manipulation and may inspire further studies on transition-based quantum error correction or measurement-based quantum computing. The paper's focus on theoretical foundations provides a basis for future experimental and applied research.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a clean and insightful contribution to the theory of multipartite entanglement by defining T states and proving their equivalence to Dicke states. While the result is mathematically elegant, the practical significance is somewhat limited by the equivalence itself, as T states do not offer new entanglement resources. However, the transition-based perspective could stimulate new ideas in quantum information processing, such as encoding information in transition patterns rather than excitation numbers. The paper is well-written and suitable for a specialized audience. Its novelty lies in the conceptual shift rather than groundbreaking results, making it a solid but incremental contribution.

title: Feature Encoding In Quantum Machine Learning: A Survey And Practical Guidelines
authors: Vincenzo Sammartino
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The encoding of classical data into quantum states constitutes the primary performance bottleneck in Quantum Machine Learning (qml) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (nisq) devices. No existing framework jointly characterises resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness, nor provides actionable selection guidelines for practitioners. This survey addresses that gap through a systematic review of 66 primary works (2017-2026) assembled via a PRISMA-adapted protocol across five academic databases. Four principal contributions are made. First, a three-axis cost-expressivity-robustness taxonomy classifies all major encoding families - basis, angle, dense-angle, amplitude, data re-uploading, and IQP - along independently measurable axes. Second, closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under nisq decoherence channels identify the critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3 below which amplitude encoding is viable. Third, a unified treatment of Fourier expressivity, barren-plateau onset, and quantum kernel concentration as functions of the encoding circuit provides the first joint trainability analysis. Fourth, a five-regime decision framework maps (D, n, p, tau) - feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type - to a hardware-grounded encoding recommendation. The central finding is that for p >= 10^-3, shallow angle-based encodings consistently outperform amplitude encoding in practice, despite the latter's exponential qubit advantage.
tldr: A survey and practical guidelines for feature encoding in quantum machine learning, focusing on cost, expressivity, and noise robustness trade-offs.
motivation: No existing framework jointly characterizes resource cost, expressivity, and noise robustness for feature encoding in QML, hindering practical selection.
method: Systematic review of 66 works (2017-2026) via PRISMA-adapted protocol; proposes a three-axis taxonomy and derives closed-form depth-fidelity bounds under decoherence.
result: Identifies critical gate-error rate p* ~ 10^-3 for amplitude encoding viability; shallow angle-based encodings outperform amplitude encoding for p >= 10^-3.
conclusion: Provides a five-regime decision framework for encoding selection based on feature dimension, qubit budget, error rate, and task type.

title: Periodic Symmetry-Adapted Encoding: Qubit Reduction In Crystalline Electronic Structure
authors: Dario Picozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the symmetry-adapted encoding (SAE) framework to periodic electronic structure, enabling qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystalline materials. By constructing a [MATH]-point supercell Hamiltonian from a folded [MATH]-point calculation and systematically identifying all applicable space-group symmetry generators -- including spin-parity, point-group, and crystal translation symmetries -- we obtain qubit Hamiltonians with fewer qubits than the Jordan--Wigner starting point. We benchmark diamond, silicon, 3C-SiC, MgO, NaCl, CsCl, h-BN, wurtzite AlN, [MATH]-quartz SiO[MATH], and MgF[MATH] using active spaces chosen to preserve complete near-degenerate frontier manifolds across cubic, hexagonal, trigonal, and tetragonal space groups. Across the suite the periodic SAE removes 4--8 qubits. The B2 CsCl benchmark realises eight independent Boolean generators, i.e. a symmetry group isomorphic to [MATH], reducing CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits. This exceeds the [MATH] maximum of molecular SAE, where only two spin parities and at most three independent Boolean point-group generators are available, because the folded crystal supplies three additional half-translation symmetries. Noiseless UCCSD-VQE benchmarks against exact diagonalisation in the active-space sector show that the reduced encodings preserve the target energies to well below chemical accuracy while reducing variational parameter counts by [MATH]--[MATH] and CNOT counts by up to [MATH]. The largest circuit savings occur when translation and point-group generators act independently in the active space, demonstrating that periodic symmetry can be converted directly into both qubit and ansatz compression. The method is implemented in the open-source QuantumSymmetry package and requires no manual specification of symmetry generators.
tldr: This paper extends symmetry-adapted encoding to periodic crystals, reducing qubit count for quantum simulations of materials.
motivation: To enable qubit-efficient quantum simulation of crystalline materials by exploiting space-group symmetries.
method: Constructs a k-point supercell Hamiltonian from folded calculations, identifies space-group symmetry generators (spin-parity, point-group, translation), and applies symmetry-adapted encoding to reduce qubit count.
result: Periodic SAE removes 4–8 qubits across various crystals; for CsCl, reduces CAS(6,7) from 14 to 6 qubits, exceeding molecular SAE limits. UCCSD-VQE benchmarks preserve chemical accuracy while reducing variational parameters and CNOT counts.
conclusion: Periodic symmetry can be directly converted into qubit and ansatz compression, offering a practical method for quantum simulation of solids.

title: Optimizing Irreversible Perturbations Of The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm
authors: Qianyu Julie Zhu, Youssef Marzouk, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos, Benjamin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Irreversible perturbations accelerate the convergence of Langevin dynamics, breaking detailed balance while preserving the invariant measure. The design of optimal irreversible perturbations has been studied in the continuous-time Gaussian setting, but extensions to non-Gaussian target distributions, and the impact of time discretization on the design of optimal perturbations, have not been well understood. Numerical discretizations of Langevin dynamics introduce bias, which is typically exacerbated by irreversible perturbations; handling this interaction demands a joint treatment of acceleration and accuracy. This paper develops a systematic framework for optimizing position-independent irreversible perturbations of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA). We formulate a constrained optimization problem that simultaneously accounts for mixing efficiency and discretization bias, where the former is characterized by a spectral gap analogue and the latter is quantified via a weighted expected squared jump distance. Within this framework, we derive an explicit characterization of the optimal position-independent irreversible perturbation. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our design yields faster convergence with controlled bias, and improves mean squared estimation errors compared to other choices of irreversible perturbation.
tldr: This paper optimizes irreversible perturbations for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm to accelerate mixing while controlling discretization bias.
motivation: Irreversible perturbations can speed up Langevin dynamics but interact poorly with time discretization, introducing bias. Prior work focused on continuous-time Gaussian targets; this paper extends to non-Gaussian targets and discrete-time algorithms.
method: The authors formulate a constrained optimization problem balancing mixing efficiency (via a spectral gap analogue) and discretization bias (via weighted expected squared jump distance), and derive the optimal position-independent irreversible perturbation.
result: An explicit characterization of the optimal perturbation is obtained, and numerical experiments show faster convergence with controlled bias and improved mean squared estimation errors compared to other perturbations.
conclusion: The framework provides a principled way to design irreversible perturbations for ULA, with potential applications in sampling and Bayesian inference. Future work may extend to position-dependent perturbations or other discretization schemes.

title: Disentangling Anomaly-Free Symmetries Of Quantum Spin Chains
authors: Sahand Seifnashri And Wilbur Shirley
abstract:
Author(s): Sahand Seifnashri and Wilbur Shirley

result: In 1+1d, all finite internal anomaly-free symmetries are onsiteable; in 2d, counterexamples exist where anomaly-free symmetries are not onsiteable.
