title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: The paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into fixed invariants (shapes) and bosonic excitations, applied to lithium's quartet state, but does not directly address the user's research interests.
motivation: To characterize the information content of three-fermion highest-spin states and understand the role of the Pauli principle in shaping wave functions.
method: Formal decomposition of wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations; applied to a benchmark-quality wave function of lithium's lowest-energy quartet state.
result: The wave function reduces to eleven shape blocks, only five numerically significant, demonstrating a compact characterization.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in identifying robust few-particle entangled states.

title: Tensor Cross Interpolation Of Purities In Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Dmytro Kolisnyk, Raimel A. Medina, Romain Vasseur, And Maksym Serbyn
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2114 (2026).

A defining feature of quantum many-body systems is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with the number of degrees of freedom. This exponential complexity naïvely renders a complete state characterization, for instance via the complete set of bipartite Renyi entropies for all disjoint regions, a challenging task. Recently, a compact way of storing subregions' purities by encoding them as amplitudes of a fictitious quantum wave function, known as entanglement feature, was proposed. Notably, the entanglement feature can be a simple object even for highly entangled quantum states. However the complexity and practical usage of the entanglement feature for general quantum states has not been explored. In this work, we demonstrate that the entanglement feature can be efficiently learned using only a polynomial amount of samples in the number of degrees of freedom through the so-called tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm, assuming it is expressible as a finite bond dimension MPS. We benchmark this learning process on Haar and random MPS states, confirming analytic expectations. Applying the TCI algorithm to quantum eigenstates of various one dimensional quantum systems, we identify cases where eigenstates have entanglement feature learnable with TCI. We conclude with possible applications of the learned entanglement feature, such as quantifying the distance between different entanglement patterns and finding the optimal one-dimensional ordering of physical indices in a given state, highlighting the potential utility of the proposed purity interpolation method.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a tensor cross interpolation method to efficiently learn the entanglement feature (purities of all subregions) of quantum many-body states, assuming it can be represented as a matrix product state.
motivation: Characterizing quantum many-body states via all bipartite Renyi entropies is exponentially hard; the entanglement feature offers a compact representation, but its practical learning for general states was unexplored.
method: The authors use tensor cross interpolation (TCI) to learn the entanglement feature as a matrix product state from a polynomial number of samples, and benchmark on Haar random states and random MPS, then apply to eigenstates of 1D quantum systems.
result: TCI can efficiently learn the entanglement feature for states where it is expressible as a finite bond dimension MPS; they identify cases in 1D eigenstates where this holds.
conclusion: The learned entanglement feature enables quantifying distances between entanglement patterns and finding optimal 1D ordering of indices, with potential applications in quantum many-body physics.

title: Phase-Sensitive Measurements On A Fermi–Hubbard Quantum Processor
authors: Alberto R. Cavallar, Luis Escalera-Moreno, Titus Franz, Timon Hilker, J. Ignacio Cirac, Philipp M. Preiss, And Benjamin F. Schiffer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2103 (2026).

Fermionic quantum processors are a promising platform for quantum simulation of correlated fermionic matter. In this work, we study a hardware-efficient protocol for measuring complex expectation values of the time-evolution operator, commonly referred to as Loschmidt echoes, with fermions in an optical superlattice. We analyze the algorithm for the Fermi–Hubbard model at half-filling as well as at finite doping. The method relies on global quench dynamics and short imaginary time evolution, the latter being realized by architecture-tailored pulse sequences starting from a product state of plaquettes. Our numerical results show that complex Loschmidt echoes can be efficiently obtained for large many-body states over a broad spectral range. This allows one to measure spectral properties of the Fermi–Hubbard model, such as the local density of states, and paves the way for the study of finite-temperature properties in current fermionic quantum simulators.

.
tldr: This paper presents a protocol for measuring Loschmidt echoes on a fermionic quantum processor to study spectral properties of the Fermi-Hubbard model.
motivation: To enable measurement of complex expectation values and spectral properties in fermionic quantum simulators, which are crucial for understanding correlated fermionic matter.
method: The protocol uses global quench dynamics and short imaginary time evolution realized by pulse sequences on an optical superlattice, starting from a product state of plaquettes.
result: Numerical results show that complex Loschmidt echoes can be efficiently obtained for large many-body states over a broad spectral range, allowing measurement of the local density of states.
conclusion: The work paves the way for studying finite-temperature properties in current fermionic quantum simulators, but does not directly address the user's specific interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, or quantum communication.

title: Interference-induced Suppression Of Doublon Transport And Prethermalization In The Extended Bose-Hubbard Model
authors: Zhen-Ting Bao, Kai Xu, And Heng Fan
abstract:
Author(s): Zhen-Ting Bao, Kai Xu, and Heng Fan

The coherent mobility of doublons, arising from second-order virtual dissociation-recombination processes, fundamentally limits their use as information carriers in the strongly interacting Bose-Hubbard model. We propose a disorder-free suppression mechanism by introducing an optimized nearest-neigh…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214306] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a disorder-free mechanism to suppress doublon transport in the extended Bose-Hubbard model via optimized nearest-neighbor interactions, leading to prethermalization.
motivation: Doublons in the strongly interacting Bose-Hubbard model have limited mobility due to second-order virtual processes, hindering their use as information carriers. The research aims to find a suppression mechanism without disorder.
method: The authors introduce an optimized nearest-neighbor interaction in the extended Bose-Hubbard model and analyze the resulting doublon dynamics using theoretical and numerical methods.
result: They find that the interference from the nearest-neighbor interaction can suppress doublon transport and induce prethermalization, even in the absence of disorder.
conclusion: The mechanism provides a new way to control doublon mobility, which may have implications for quantum information transport in lattice systems, though direct applications to the user's interests are limited.

title: Diagnosing Chaos With Projected Ensembles Of Process Tensors
authors: Peter O’donovan, Neil Dowling, Kavan Modi, And Mark T. Mitchison
abstract:
Author(s): Peter O’Donovan, Neil Dowling, Kavan Modi, and Mark T. Mitchison

An approach to probing quantum chaos by repeated interventions is shown to unify techniques for the study and simulation of many-body quantum dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020322] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a method to diagnose quantum chaos using projected ensembles of process tensors, unifying techniques for many-body quantum dynamics.
motivation: To develop a unified framework for probing quantum chaos through repeated interventions, which can be applied to study and simulate many-body quantum systems.
method: The approach uses projected ensembles of process tensors, which are mathematical objects that capture the effect of repeated measurements or interventions on a quantum system.
result: The method provides a way to diagnose chaos by analyzing the statistical properties of the projected ensemble, linking to known signatures of chaos.
conclusion: The work offers a new tool for characterizing chaos in quantum many-body systems, with potential applications in quantum simulation and information processing.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras of QAOA circuits for cycle and complete graphs, proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs and giving explicit DLA dimensions and bases.
motivation: To understand the trainability and expressiveness of QAOA, particularly the presence of barren plateaus, which hinder variational quantum algorithms.
method: Analytical derivation of DLA dimensions, centers, and decompositions for general graphs, with explicit calculations for cycle and complete graphs using Lie algebra theory.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a 1D center and a semisimple component isomorphic to multiple copies of su(2), leading to a closed-form variance of the cost function and proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is n^2 - 1 with an explicit basis.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA trainability, but the focus is on specific graph types and does not directly address the user's research interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid systems.

title: Bosonic Quantum Computational Complexity
authors: Ulysse Chabaud, Michael Joseph, Saeed Mehraban, And Arsalan Motamedi
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2110 (2026).

Quantum computing involving physical systems with continuous degrees of freedom, such as the quantum states of light, has recently attracted significant interest. However, a well-defined quantum complexity theory for these bosonic computations over infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces is missing. In this work, we lay foundations for such a research program. We introduce natural complexity classes and problems based on bosonic generalizations of BQP, the local Hamiltonian problem, and QMA. We uncover several relationships and subtle differences between standard Boolean classical and discrete variable quantum complexity classes and identify outstanding open problems. In particular: 1. We show that the power of quadratic (Gaussian) quantum dynamics is equivalent to the class BQL. More generally, we define classes of continuous-variable quantum polynomial time computations with a bounded probability of error based on higher-degree gates. Due to the infinite dimensional Hilbert space, it is not a priori clear whether a decidable upper bound can be obtained for these classes. We identify complete problems for these classes and demonstrate a BQP lower and EXPSPACE upper bound. We further show that the problem of computing expectation values of polynomial bosonic observables is in PSPACE. 2. We prove that the problem of deciding the boundedness of the spectrum of a bosonic Hamiltonian is co-NP-hard. Furthermore, we show that the problem of finding the minimum energy of a bosonic Hamiltonian critically depends on the non-Gaussian stellar rank of the family of energy-constrained states one optimizes over: for constant stellar rank, it is NP-complete; for polynomially-bounded rank, it is in QMA; for unbounded rank, it is undecidable.

.
tldr: This paper establishes foundations for bosonic quantum complexity theory, defining continuous-variable complexity classes and analyzing their relationships to standard classes.
motivation: Quantum computing with continuous-variable systems (e.g., light) lacks a well-defined complexity theory, hindering understanding of their computational power.
method: The authors introduce bosonic generalizations of BQP, QMA, and the local Hamiltonian problem, and analyze their computational complexity using techniques from quantum information and computational complexity theory.
result: Gaussian quantum dynamics is equivalent to BQL; higher-degree gate classes have BQP lower and EXPSPACE upper bounds; expectation values of polynomial observables are in PSPACE; bosonic Hamiltonian problems range from NP-complete to undecidable depending on stellar rank.
conclusion: This work opens a new research direction in quantum complexity theory for continuous-variable systems, with many open problems remaining.

title: Fully Optimised Variational Simulation Of A Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition On A Trapped-ion Quantum Computer
authors: Lesley Gover, Vinul Wimalaweera, Fariha Azad, Matthew Decross, Michael Foss-Feig, And Andrew G. Green
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2109 (2026).

We time-evolve a translationally invariant quantum state on the Quantinuum H1-1 trapped-ion quantum processor, studying the dynamical quantum phase transition of the transverse field Ising model. This physics requires a delicate cancellation of phases in the many-body wavefunction and presents a tough challenge for current quantum devices. We follow the dynamics using a quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz, optimised for the time-evolution using a fidelity cost function. Sampling costs are mitigated by using the measured values of this circuit as stochastic corrections to a simple classical extrapolation of the ansatz parameters. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of variational quantum time-evolution and reveal a hitherto hidden simplicity of the evolution of the transverse-field Ising model through the dynamical quantum phase transition.

.
tldr: This paper demonstrates variational quantum time-evolution of the transverse field Ising model on a trapped-ion quantum processor to study a dynamical quantum phase transition.
motivation: To test the feasibility of variational quantum simulation on current noisy quantum devices for a challenging many-body problem requiring delicate phase cancellation.
method: A quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz is optimized using a fidelity cost function, with sampling costs mitigated by using measured circuit values as stochastic corrections to a classical extrapolation of ansatz parameters.
result: The variational approach successfully followed the dynamics through the dynamical quantum phase transition, revealing a hidden simplicity in the evolution of the transverse-field Ising model.
conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of variational quantum time-evolution on current hardware and suggest that such methods can uncover simplifying structures in complex quantum dynamics.

title: Optimizing Qubo On A Quantum Computer By Mimicking Imaginary Time Evolution
authors: Yahui Chai And Alice Di Tucci
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm for solving quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems using an imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuit (ITEMC). The circuit parameters are optimized to mimic short-time ITE, using only single- and two-qubit expectation values. This significantly reduces the measurement overhead by avoiding full energy evaluation. By updating the initial state based on results from last step iteratively, the algorithm quickly converges to the low-energy solutions. With a pre-sorting step that optimizes quantum gate ordering based on QUBO coefficients, the convergence is further improved. Our classical simulations achieve approximation ratios above up to 150 qubits. Furthermore, the linear scaling of entanglement entropy with system size suggests that the circuit is challenging to simulate classically using tensor networks. We also demonstrate hardware runs on IBM’s device for 40, 60, and 80 qubits, and obtain solutions compatible with that from simulated annealing.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for QUBO problems using imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuits.
motivation: To solve QUBO problems on near-term quantum devices with reduced measurement overhead and improved convergence.
method: Optimizes circuit parameters to mimic short-time imaginary time evolution using only single- and two-qubit expectation values, with iterative initial state updates and pre-sorting of gate ordering.
result: Achieves approximation ratios above 0.9 for up to 150 qubits in simulation, and demonstrates hardware runs on IBM devices for 40, 60, and 80 qubits.
conclusion: The algorithm shows promise for QUBO on quantum computers, but its relevance to the user's interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid systems is indirect.

title: Reply To "Interpreting Bohm Quantum Potentials In `Computing Quantum Waves Exactly From Classical Action'"
authors: Gabor Vattay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recent arXiv posting arXiv:2605.20443 by Lohmiller and Slotine attempts to address the omission of the Bohm quantum potential in their proposed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schr\"odinger equation. They introduce a position-dependent time transformation to argue that the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel. A rigorous mathematical examination of this transformation reveals a violation of the multivariable chain rule. The spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical reference frame. The mathematical framework presented by the authors remains identical to the well-established semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact exclusively for quadratic potentials.
tldr: This paper is a technical reply refuting a claimed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation, showing the proposed transformation violates the chain rule and reduces to the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator.
motivation: To correct a mathematical error in a previous claim that classical action can exactly reproduce quantum mechanics without the Bohm quantum potential.
method: Rigorous mathematical examination of the position-dependent time transformation proposed by Lohmiller and Slotine, checking the multivariable chain rule and comparing with the Van Vleck propagator.
result: The transformation violates the chain rule, spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude do not vanish in the physical frame, and the framework is identical to the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials.
conclusion: The claimed exact equivalence is invalid; the semiclassical approximation remains the correct description for non-quadratic potentials.

title: xCPS: An xAct Package For Covariant Phase Space, Noether Charges, And Entropy
authors: Juan Margalef-Bentabol
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: xCPS is an xAct tensor algebra package for symbolic computations within the covariant phase space formalism of field theories. From a generic Lagrangian, xCPS automates the derivation of equations of motion and symplectic currents. It systematically determines whether an infinitesimal transformation in the space of fields is a Noether symmetry and computes the associated Noether charge. Additionally, xCPS can in many cases determine whether a tensorial expression is a divergence and, if so, find its divergence potential. By implementing vertical exterior calculus through a graded, supercommutative wedge product and vertical operators, the package enables efficient computations in gauge theories and higher-derivative models of gravity, including the derivation of thermodynamic quantities like Wald's entropy. xCPS is open-source under the GPL license and available at [URL].
tldr: xCPS is a software package for symbolic computations in covariant phase space formalism, automating derivation of equations of motion, Noether charges, and Wald entropy.
motivation: To provide a computational tool for researchers working on covariant phase space methods, especially in gauge theories and higher-derivative gravity.
method: Implements vertical exterior calculus via a graded wedge product and vertical operators within the xAct tensor algebra framework.
result: The package automates derivation of symplectic currents, Noether symmetries and charges, divergence potentials, and thermodynamic quantities like Wald entropy.
conclusion: xCPS facilitates efficient symbolic computations in covariant phase space, aiding research in gravity and field theories, but is a computational tool rather than a new physical result.

title: Isospectrality And Operator Complexity
authors: Pradip Kattel, Yicheng Tang, Natan Andrei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains, one strongly interacting and one quadratic, that nevertheless display remarkably different phase structures and operator dynamics. A nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation maps one onto the other while preserving the entire many-body spectrum and converting local fermion operators into extended many-body strings. Thus, operators that evolve within a closed linear subspace in the quadratic model become interacting operators that generate increasingly higher-body terms and exhibit asymptotic Lanczos growth [MATH]. Despite their identical spectra, the two models realize distinct phases and sharply different notions of operator complexity. Our results demonstrate that free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible.
tldr: The paper shows that two isospectral fermion chains, one interacting and one quadratic, have identical spectra but vastly different operator complexity and phase structures.
motivation: To understand how operator complexity can differ despite identical spectra, challenging the notion that free spectra imply simple dynamics.
method: They construct a nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation mapping a quadratic fermion chain to a strongly interacting one, preserving the spectrum but converting local operators into many-body strings.
result: The quadratic model exhibits linear Lanczos growth, while the interacting model shows asymptotic Lanczos growth, indicating fundamentally different operator complexity despite isospectrality.
conclusion: Free many-body spectra are compatible with interacting operator dynamics, highlighting that spectral information alone does not determine dynamical complexity.

title: Setting Angles In Quantum Approximate Optimization At Utility-scale
authors: Maosheng Guo, Joel Jurado Diaz, Anurag Ramesh, Conrad J. Haupt, Alberto Baiardi, Dimitrios Athanasakos, M. Emre Sahin, Oscar Wallis, George Pennington, Christian Arenz, Sebastian Brandhofer, Georgios Korpas, Ieva \v{c}epait\.e, J. A. Monta\~nez-Barrera, Jakub Marecek, Davide Venturelli, Stephan Eidenbenz, David E. Bernal Neira, Daniel J. Egger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a powerful heuristic that seeks to solve combinatorial optimization problems using quantum hardware and classical optimization in tandem. Various methods exist to train the parameterized quantum circuits that serve as an ansatz in QAOA. However, which method works best to identify optimal angles for a given problem instance remains poorly understood, especially at utility-scale, i.e., [MATH] qubits or more. In this work, we address this challenge through utility-scale benchmarks from which we distill operational guidance for QAOA practitioners. First, we investigate approximation techniques, such as matrix product states and Pauli propagation, to find optimal angles. Second, we train QAOA on small-scale representative problems and transfer the angles to larger ones. We then validate the results on quantum hardware for utility-scale problem instances that can be meaningfully executed. In this way, we identify insights for QAOA angle setting strategies that work best for problems at the utility scale, including as a function of resource cost for the search. Crucially, the operational implications we draw from our benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines efficiently on current and future hardware.
tldr: This paper benchmarks angle-setting strategies for QAOA at utility-scale (100+ qubits) using classical approximations and angle transfer, but does not address the user's specific interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, quantum communication, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To determine which methods for finding optimal QAOA angles work best at large problem sizes, as this is poorly understood and critical for practical quantum optimization.
method: The authors compare approximation techniques (matrix product states, Pauli propagation) and angle transfer from small to large instances, then validate on quantum hardware for utility-scale problems.
result: They identify operational insights for QAOA angle setting strategies that work best at utility scale, including resource cost trade-offs.
conclusion: The findings provide guidance for practitioners to efficiently execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines on current and future hardware.

title: Multi-Qubit Dyadic Phase Fixing For Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation
authors: Justin Kalloor, Mathias Weiden, Ed Younis, John Kubiatowicz, Costin Iancu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires translating application-level quantum circuits into the Clifford+[MATH] gate set, where the [MATH] gate is the dominant resource cost. Phase kickback is an ancilla-based technique that can dramatically reduce [MATH]-count for rotations with dyadic angles, but has previously been limited to highly structured circuit families. We present Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), a general multi-qubit synthesis tool that extends phase kickback to general quantum circuits. DPF uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any input circuit. Combined with a decision matrix to automatically size the final phase gradient register, our end-to-end workflow achieves up to 70% reduction in [MATH]-count compared to and up to 60% compared to Repeat-Until-Success synthesis on a diverse set of benchmarks. We map these compiled circuits to a surface-code architecture to evaluate space-time volume, demonstrating up to a 60\% reduction in this metric as well. However, for some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverge significantly, demonstrating that [MATH]-count alone is a useful but incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant program costs.
tldr: This paper presents a method to reduce T-gate count in fault-tolerant quantum circuits by extending phase kickback to general circuits via numerical unitary synthesis.
motivation: T-gates are expensive in fault-tolerant quantum computing, and existing phase kickback techniques are limited to structured circuits. The authors aim to generalize this approach to arbitrary circuits.
method: They introduce Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), which uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any circuit, combined with a decision matrix to size the phase gradient register.
result: DPF achieves up to 70% reduction in T-count and up to 60% reduction in space-time volume on diverse benchmarks compared to prior methods.
conclusion: The method significantly reduces resource costs for fault-tolerant quantum compilation, but T-count alone is an incomplete proxy for actual costs.

title: Newton's Identity In Finite-Bead Fermionic Partition Function
authors: J. Valenzuela A. Chaudhary
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For non-interacting fermions in a harmonic trap, the partition function at any discrete number of imaginary time slices (or beads) and for any choice of short-time propagator admits an exact recursion relation derived directly from the contracted determinant form of the path integral. This finite-bead recursion is distinct from earlier continuum-limit recursions, which do not apply to the discrete time partition functions. By identifying a direct correspondence between this recursion and Newton's identity, application of a closed-form result from the theory of partitions provides an exact expression for the one-dimensional [MATH]-fermion finite-bead partition function. From this, the Thermodynamic and Hamiltonian energies and specific heats are analytically calculated for any [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and propagator choice.
tldr: This paper derives exact finite-bead partition functions for non-interacting fermions in a harmonic trap using Newton's identity.
motivation: To obtain exact expressions for the partition function at finite imaginary time slices, which are not captured by continuum-limit recursions.
method: The authors derive a recursion relation from the contracted determinant form of the path integral and identify it with Newton's identity, then apply a closed-form result from partition theory.
result: Exact one-dimensional N-fermion finite-bead partition function, from which thermodynamic and Hamiltonian energies and specific heats are analytically calculated for any N, beads, temperature, and propagator choice.
conclusion: The work provides a new exact tool for finite-temperature path integral simulations of non-interacting fermions, but its direct relevance to the user's interests in quantum information and hybrid systems is limited.

title: Decoder-Consistent Hamiltonians For POVM-Based Quantum Relaxations
authors: Takayuki Suzuki
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In compression-based quantum relaxations like QRAO, classical variables are encoded into qubits and decoded after optimization. We formalize that the choice of the quantum Hamiltonian is fundamentally determined by this decoder. By representing the decoder as a POVM, we define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. Using this framework, we reveal that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions, and we provide new approximation guarantees for the MaxCut problem based directly on POVM decoder design.
tldr: This paper formalizes decoder-consistent Hamiltonians for POVM-based quantum relaxations, revealing inconsistencies in standard QRAO Hamiltonians and providing new approximation guarantees for MaxCut.
motivation: To address inconsistencies in quantum relaxation optimization (QRAO) Hamiltonians for mixed-degree quadratic functions and to provide a principled framework for Hamiltonian design based on decoder POVMs.
method: The authors represent the decoder as a POVM and define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. They analyze standard QRAO Hamiltonians and derive approximation guarantees for MaxCut.
result: Standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions. New approximation guarantees for MaxCut are provided based directly on POVM decoder design.
conclusion: The framework enables systematic construction of consistent Hamiltonians for quantum relaxations, with implications for optimization algorithms on quantum computers.

title: Broadband Chromatic Dispersion Of Thermo-refractive Coefficients And Its Impact In Silicon Nitride Nonlinear Photonics
authors: Shao-Chien Ou, Gregory Moille, Kartik Srinivasan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The thermo-refractive effect is a cornerstone of frequency and phase tuning in photonic integrated circuits. In particular, it enables control of phase-matching for integrated nonlinear processes. Chromatic dispersion of the group and effective refractive indices and modal confinement are standard considerations in design, but material thermo-refractive coefficients (TRCs) are typically taken to be fixed for the guiding and cladding materials. Here, we demonstrate that the assumption of non-dispersive TRCs across an octave of bandwidth between the telecom and visible results in a significant discrepancy between measured and simulated resonance frequencies of an integrated Si3N4/SiO2 microring resonator. We uncover a 7 % variation in Si3N4 and SiO2 material TRCs across this range, finding that the variation of dneff /dT from material TRCs is 1.3 times that from modal confinement. This accurately matches a temperature-dependent Lorentz oscillator model describing their chromatic dispersion. By integrating these dispersive TRCs into a multi-physics finite-element model, we achieve precise correspondence with experimentally measured temperature-dependent resonance frequency shifts across the octave, including in the context of second harmonic generation devices. Our results provide a physical framework and a universal predictive workflow for the design of high-efficiency, multi-wavelength nonlinear optical processes, fundamentally improving the thermal control of integrated photonic devices.
tldr: This paper investigates the chromatic dispersion of thermo-refractive coefficients in Si3N4/SiO2 microring resonators and its impact on nonlinear photonics, showing that dispersive TRCs are necessary for accurate modeling across an octave bandwidth.
motivation: Thermo-refractive coefficients are typically assumed non-dispersive, but this assumption leads to discrepancies between measured and simulated resonance frequencies over a wide bandwidth. The research aims to characterize and model the dispersion of TRCs to improve thermal control in integrated photonic devices.
method: The authors use a temperature-dependent Lorentz oscillator model to describe the chromatic dispersion of TRCs and integrate it into a multi-physics finite-element model. They compare simulated temperature-dependent resonance frequency shifts with experimental measurements from Si3N4/SiO2 microring resonators.
result: They find a 7% variation in Si3N4 and SiO2 material TRCs across the telecom-to-visible octave, and that the variation of dneff/dT from material TRCs is 1.3 times that from modal confinement. The dispersive TRC model accurately matches experimental data.
conclusion: The work provides a physical framework and predictive workflow for designing high-efficiency, multi-wavelength nonlinear optical processes, improving thermal control of integrated photonic devices.

title: Symmetries And Overparametrization Properties Of Hamiltonian Variational Ansatzes For The $(1+1)$d $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Lattice Gauge Theory
authors: Kanta Yamanaka, Takanori Daiza, Katsumi Imaizumi, Yutaro Iiyama, Lento Nagano, Ryu Sawada, Koji Terashi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We perform detailed studies of five Hamiltonian variational ansatzes (HVA) based on the Hamiltonian of the [MATH]d [MATH] lattice gauge theory. The ansatzes are designed to respect local and global symmetries of the original Hamiltonian and therefore act on a finely segmented state Hilbert space. Following Larocca et al. (2023), we numerically study the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) and the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) of the ansatzes within specific invariant subspaces. The ansatzes all involve sums of weight-three Paulis in their generators, which is a feature that have so far been underexplored in this context. We also perform numerical experiments to determine the ground state energy of the original Hamiltonian via variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and observe that overparametrization of the ansatzes coincides with the apparent disappearance of local minima in the loss function, in line with the finding in the reference. Finally, the decay rate of the VQE loss function under gradient descent optimization is revealed to scale linearly with the number of parameters in the ansatz. These results help to enrich the theory of overparameterization of quantum circuits and inform the design of scalable variational ansatzes.
tldr: This paper studies symmetries and overparametrization properties of Hamiltonian variational ansatzes for (1+1)d Z2 lattice gauge theory, focusing on dynamical Lie algebra and quantum Fisher information matrix.
motivation: To understand overparametrization in quantum circuits and design scalable variational ansatzes for lattice gauge theories.
method: Numerical study of dynamical Lie algebra dimension and QFIM rank for five HVA ansatzes, plus VQE ground state energy optimization.
result: Overparametrization coincides with disappearance of local minima; loss function decay rate scales linearly with number of parameters.
conclusion: Results enrich theory of overparametrization and inform design of scalable variational ansatzes.

title: Towards Stable And Accurate Electron Dynamics Via Neural Network Based Time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo
authors: Weizhong Fu, Zhe Li, Yubing Qian, Ruichen Li, Weiluo Ren, Ji Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time dynamics of interacting electrons lies at the interface between quantum mechanics and non-equilibrium physics, governing the microscopic origin of ultrafast phenomena of molecules and nano-materials. Though neural network variational Monte Carlo has achieved unprecedented accuracy for stationary state calculations, its extension to real-time evolution remains challenging. In this work, we introduce the neural basis time-dependent variational Monte Carlo framework, which achieves stable and highly accurate simulations of electron dynamics. By constraining the time evolution to a compact, customized manifold spanned by the neural basis, we effectively bypass instability issues and achieve long-term stable evolution. Moreover, we demonstrate that this framework yields benchmark-quality accuracy in simulating the laser-driven dipole responses of the hydrogen atom and a stretched hydrogen molecule, and accurately extracts the dynamic polarizabilities of helium and beryllium atoms. Our work reveals the vast potential of neural network wavefunctions for accurately describing real-time electron dynamics and establishes a promising new route for first-principles simulations of complex, time-dependent electronic phenomena.
tldr: This paper introduces a neural network-based time-dependent variational Monte Carlo method for stable and accurate simulation of electron dynamics.
motivation: Real-time dynamics of interacting electrons is crucial for understanding ultrafast phenomena, but extending neural network variational Monte Carlo to real-time evolution has been challenging due to instability issues.
method: The authors propose a neural basis time-dependent variational Monte Carlo framework that constrains time evolution to a compact manifold spanned by a neural basis, bypassing instability and enabling long-term stable evolution.
result: The method achieves benchmark-quality accuracy in simulating laser-driven dipole responses of hydrogen atom and stretched hydrogen molecule, and accurately extracts dynamic polarizabilities of helium and beryllium atoms.
conclusion: This work demonstrates the potential of neural network wavefunctions for real-time electron dynamics and opens a new route for first-principles simulations of time-dependent electronic phenomena.

title: Symmetry-adapted Qubit Encoding With Complete Active Space And Bravyi--Kitaev Mapping For Quantum Chemistry On A Quantum Computer
authors: Jonathan Tennyson Dario Picozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) for quantum chemistry on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors. Building on exact-symmetry encodings, we extend symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate [MATH]-symmetries corresponding to frozen-core and virtual orbitals, thereby reducing qubit requirements without significant loss of accuracy. We derive the mapping from the second-quantised Hamiltonian to active-space qubit Hamiltonians, prove its equivalence to the canonical CAS Hamiltonian with frozen-core and virtual-orbital projection, and integrate it with point-group and spin-parity symmetry encodings via affine Clifford transformations to maximise qubit reduction while preserving the target symmetry sector. The same framework also accommodates the Bravyi--Kitaev mapping, yielding an SAE-CAS-BK variant that is unitarily equivalent to SAE-CAS. Numerical benchmarking on nine small molecules using UCCSD and a hardware-efficient shifted-circular-alternating (HE-SCA) ansatz shows that SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts and Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, and often accelerates VQE convergence; with HE-SCA it consistently reaches CAS reference energies in cases where JW-CAS does not converge within the tested budgets. We provide an open-source implementation in the Python package QuantumSymmetry. SAE-CAS offers a route to resource-efficient molecular simulations on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors.
tldr: This paper presents a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding method for quantum chemistry on quantum computers, reducing qubit requirements via frozen-core and virtual orbital approximations.
motivation: To reduce qubit and circuit requirements for quantum chemistry simulations on near-term and fault-tolerant quantum processors.
method: Extends symmetry-adapted encodings to approximate symmetries (frozen-core/virtual orbitals), integrates with point-group and spin-parity symmetries via affine Clifford transformations, and incorporates Bravyi-Kitaev mapping.
result: SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts, Pauli weight, and circuit depth; with HE-SCA ansatz it converges to CAS reference energies where JW-CAS fails.
conclusion: Provides a resource-efficient route for molecular simulations on quantum computers, with open-source implementation.

title: Single-Frequency Symmetry-Empowered Through-Barrier Sensing In Reconfigurable Complex Media
authors: Shuai S. A. Yuan, Viktar Asadchy, Philipp Del Hougne
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mirror symmetry can strongly enhance the transmission of waves through a barrier inside a complex medium. We recently showed that this phenomenon enables quantitative through-barrier sensing: by tuning programmable scatterers on one side of the barrier to maximize the broadband total transmission through the barrier, the characteristics of scatterers at mirror-symmetric positions on the other side of the barrier can be determined. Considering a sufficiently large bandwidth was crucial to ensure that no accidental narrowband asymmetric resonance can outperform the symmetry-induced transmission enhancement. Here, we overcome this scheme's vexing need for a large bandwidth by replacing the underlying frequency diversity with configurational diversity. Specifically, we introduce auxiliary tunable scatterers at mirror-symmetric positions on either side of the barrier and sweep their characteristics through a series of random mirror-symmetric configurations. We tune the programmable main scatterers on one side of the barrier to maximize the average of the total through-barrier transmission over a series of configurations of the auxiliary scatterers at a single frequency, in order to sense the characteristics of the main scatterers on the other side of the barrier. We systematically study the accuracy of our single-frequency sensing scheme based on a multiport-network system model that cascades two mirror-related wave-chaotic cavities with a weakly transmitting barrier in between. We further examine an extension to non-reciprocal chaotic cavities involving circulators. Altogether, our results establish configurational diversity as a route to single-frequency, symmetry-empowered through-barrier sensing in reconfigurable complex media.
tldr: This paper uses configurational diversity at a single frequency to perform through-barrier sensing in complex media, replacing the need for broadband measurements.
motivation: Previous symmetry-enhanced through-barrier sensing required large bandwidth to avoid accidental asymmetric resonances; the authors aim to eliminate this bandwidth requirement.
method: They introduce auxiliary tunable scatterers at mirror-symmetric positions on both sides of the barrier and sweep their configurations randomly. The main programmable scatterers are tuned to maximize average total transmission over these configurations at a single frequency.
result: The single-frequency scheme achieves accurate sensing of scatterer characteristics, as demonstrated with a multiport-network model of two mirror-related wave-chaotic cavities separated by a weak barrier, and extended to non-reciprocal cavities with circulators.
conclusion: Configurational diversity enables single-frequency symmetry-empowered through-barrier sensing, potentially simplifying experimental implementations and broadening applicability.

title: A Comprehensive Survey On Semantic Communication In Non-Terrestrial Networks: Architectures, Methodologies, And Challenges
authors: Loc X. Nguyen, Avi Deb Raha, Huy Q. Le, Zhu Han, Eui-Nam Huh, Choong Seon Hong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sixth-generation wireless networks are envisioned to deliver ubiquitous, seamless, and intelligent connectivity that reaches far beyond the limits of terrestrial infrastructure. Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) are central to this vision, extending coverage to underserved regions, remote terrain, and disaster zones that terrestrial deployment cannot economically reach. However, NTN architecture faces numerous limitations: severe path loss over long distances, long propagation delays, large and time-varying Doppler shifts, limited visibility windows, and tight on-board energy and computing budgets. Semantic communication (SemCom), which conveys the meaning of data rather than its raw bit-level representation, is unusually well matched to these conditions: extreme compression rate for task-oriented eases bandwidth scarcity, deep joint source-channel coding prevents the cliff effect due to low signal-to-noise ratio, and generative-AI reconstructs content from sparse cues that survive rain-faded or blocked links. This observation, that each NTN limitation maps onto a SemCom property that addresses it, motivates our survey. We first walk through the NTN limitations one by one, pairing each with the SemCom design choices that complement it, then we organize the literature along three axes: the NTN platform, the semantic methodology, and the supporting techniques, and follow this with platform-by-platform deep dives on satellite-centric, UAV/HAPS-centric, and integrated SAGIN systems. The survey concludes by identifying open research problems, gaps in existing standards, and future directions, including the application of foundation models, energy-aware scheduling, and quantum-assisted SemCom for deep space communication.
tldr: A survey on semantic communication in non-terrestrial networks, mapping NTN limitations to SemCom advantages.
motivation: NTNs face severe path loss, delays, Doppler shifts, and energy constraints; SemCom offers extreme compression and robustness.
method: Literature survey organized by NTN platform, semantic methodology, and supporting techniques.
result: Identifies that each NTN limitation can be addressed by a SemCom property; reviews satellite, UAV/HAPS, and integrated SAGIN systems.
conclusion: Open problems include foundation models, energy-aware scheduling, and quantum-assisted SemCom for deep space.

title: Gradient Descent At The Edge Of Stability: Free Energy Model And Kinetic Description Of The Two-layer Network
authors: Antonin Chodron de Courcel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dynamics of gradient descent in the Edge of Stability regime, where the learning rate is large enough to induce persistent oscillations in the loss and the sharpness. We propose a continuous-time effective model that tracks the evolution of the average trajectory coupled with the time-averaged covariance of its fast oscillations. Our analysis reveals that the natural quantity to monitor in such unstable regimes is an effective free energy, which combines the original risk functional with a curvature-related "entropic" term. Our model allows us to track the envelope of the oscillations even in situations where its dynamics evolve on similar timescales as the averaged weights. Otherwise stated, we can track the spikes that occur during the training of some neural network architectures. For wide two-layer neural networks optimized under stable non-vanishing oscillations, we derive a mean-field limit that results in a novel kinetic equation describing the joint distribution of weights and their fluctuations. We show that this equation can be interpreted as a Wasserstein-2 gradient flow of a macroscopic free energy. Finally, we provide numerical evidence on matrix factorization and deep learning tasks (CIFAR-10) to demonstrate the model's accuracy in capturing the envelope of the oscillations and the predictive power of the effective free energy.
tldr: This paper studies gradient descent dynamics in the Edge of Stability regime using a free energy model and kinetic description for two-layer neural networks.
motivation: To understand the persistent oscillations in loss and sharpness when training with large learning rates, and to develop a theoretical framework capturing these dynamics.
method: Proposes a continuous-time effective model tracking average trajectory and time-averaged covariance, and derives a mean-field limit leading to a kinetic equation for weight distribution.
result: Identifies an effective free energy combining risk and curvature-related entropy, enabling tracking of oscillation envelopes; numerical validation on matrix factorization and CIFAR-10.
conclusion: Provides a novel theoretical tool for analyzing unstable training regimes, with potential implications for understanding generalization in deep learning.

title: Automated Proving Of Shannon-Type Entropy Inequalities Via Fine-Tuned Language Models And Guided Tree Search
authors: Shing Yin Wong, Shaocheng Liu, Linqi Song, Amin Gohari, Cheuk Ting Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proving Shannon-type entropy inequalities is a fundamental task in information theory that often requires constructing non-trivial linear combinations of known constraints, which is a combinatorial search problem that scales poorly with the number of random variables. We investigate whether small-scale large language models (0.6B--1.7B parameters), fine-tuned on atomic proof steps and combined with guided beam search, can automate this process. On a held-out test set of 60 inequalities spanning n=10 to 15 variables, our 0.6B fine-tuned model achieves an 85\% proof success rate with tree search. GPT-5.5 solves 1.7\% samples under zero-shot prompting while Psitip solves 33.3\% samples. A systematic ablation study across training context length (4096 vs.\ 8192 tokens) and data distribution (n=9-skewed vs not skewed) reveals that a 4096-token not skewed training distribution yields the best performance, with extended context and skewed data providing no marginal benefit. We further identify two dominant failure modes -- format failures and step quality degradation -- and verify that the beam-scoring heuristic is essential via a controlled ablation (random scoring reduces success from 83\% to 23\%).
tldr: This paper uses fine-tuned language models and guided tree search to automate proving Shannon-type entropy inequalities, achieving 85% success on a test set.
motivation: Proving Shannon-type entropy inequalities is a combinatorial search problem that scales poorly; existing automated tools like Psitip have limited success, motivating the use of AI.
method: Small-scale LLMs (0.6B-1.7B parameters) are fine-tuned on atomic proof steps and combined with guided beam search to generate proofs; ablation studies compare training context length and data distribution.
result: The 0.6B model achieves 85% proof success rate on 60 inequalities (n=10-15), outperforming GPT-5.5 (1.7%) and Psitip (33.3%); beam-scoring heuristic is critical (random scoring drops success from 83% to 23%).
conclusion: Fine-tuned small LLMs with guided search can automate entropy inequality proving, but the approach is limited to Shannon-type inequalities and may not generalize to more complex information-theoretic tasks.

title: Compositional Boundaries For Density Fusion
authors: Ratan Bahadur Thapa, Ali Darijani, J\"urgen Beyerer, Steffen Staab
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed uncertainty-management systems often combine local probabilistic models along aggregation trees chosen by communication, privacy, or scheduling constraints. The final density should depend on the weighted sources, not on the particular order in which intermediate nodes combine them. We study this requirement as an algebraic compositionality problem for binary fusion of weighted probability densities. The central question is when a local fusion rule can be executed hierarchically while remaining order-invariant. We establish a compositional boundary for local segment-valued fusion rules. Within the class of continuous binary rules with additive output weights and weight-only coefficients, order-invariant hierarchical execution characterizes normalized weighted linear pooling; norm-induced segment balancing realizes the corresponding coefficient. Smooth endpoint-to-candidate [MATH]-divergence balancing has a different local geometry: its quadratic expansion induces square-root effective weights, showing why pairwise solvability alone is insufficient for schedule-independent fusion. We show that this obstruction is local to endpoint-to-candidate binary balancing, whereas global divergence barycenters retain additive-weight local limits. Finally, Gaussian mixtures show how the same issue appears in finite model classes: exact fusion is compositional, whereas stepwise compression is compositional only under a congruence condition on unnormalized component measures. These results distinguish exact schedule-independent fusion from global aggregation objectives and local approximation heuristics.
tldr: This paper studies order-invariant hierarchical fusion of weighted probability densities, establishing that only normalized weighted linear pooling achieves compositional invariance, while other methods like divergence balancing exhibit local obstructions.
motivation: Distributed uncertainty-management systems combine local probabilistic models along aggregation trees, and the final density should be independent of the order of combination. The paper aims to characterize when local fusion rules can be executed hierarchically while remaining order-invariant.
method: The authors formulate the problem as an algebraic compositionality problem for binary fusion of weighted probability densities. They analyze continuous binary rules with additive output weights and weight-only coefficients, and examine local geometry of divergence balancing and Gaussian mixture models.
result: Order-invariant hierarchical execution characterizes normalized weighted linear pooling; norm-induced segment balancing realizes the corresponding coefficient. Smooth endpoint-to-candidate divergence balancing has a different local geometry that prevents schedule-independent fusion, whereas global divergence barycenters retain additive-weight local limits.
conclusion: The results distinguish exact schedule-independent fusion from global aggregation objectives and local approximation heuristics, highlighting that pairwise solvability alone is insufficient for schedule-independent fusion.

title: Wave Focusing In Metamaterials: Tactile Displays Beyond The Diffraction Limit
authors: Gregory Reardon, Max Linnander, Dustin Goetz, Neeli Tummala, Yon Visell
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We address the challenge of engineering distributed haptic displays capable of reproducing multiple localized, independently addressable vibrations -- representing virtual tactile pixels -- at arbitrary locations on a surface. Our technique is based on the focusing of mechanical waves in a flexural plate using a sparse set of actuators. At tactile frequencies, wave diffraction prevents the formation of localized virtual tactile pixels at spatial scales relevant for multi-digit touch interactions. We overcome this limitation by augmenting the plate with a lattice of mechanical resonators, forming a locally resonant metamaterial plate. Coupling between the plate's dynamic modes and those of the resonators alters the dispersion relation governing wave transmission, introducing a slow-wave branch that enables focusing beyond the diffraction limit imposed by the unmodified plate. We use numerical simulations to engineer the dispersion relation of the metamaterial system for high-resolution focusing at tactile frequencies. We then fabricate a metamaterial tactile display and experimentally demonstrate virtual pixels that are far more localized than those generated on an otherwise identical plate without resonators, resulting in a tenfold reduction in virtual-pixel area. In behavioral experiments, we show that this system can deliver perceptually localized single- and multi-point tactile feedback and moving tactile sources while maintaining independent control over temporal waveforms at multiple display locations. The methods reported here can enable high-resolution haptic displays for widespread applications using a small number of actuated degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper uses locally resonant metamaterials to focus mechanical waves beyond the diffraction limit for haptic displays, achieving tenfold reduction in virtual-pixel area.
motivation: To overcome wave diffraction limits that prevent high-resolution tactile feedback in haptic displays, enabling multiple localized vibrations at arbitrary surface locations.
method: Augmenting a flexural plate with a lattice of mechanical resonators to form a locally resonant metamaterial, altering the dispersion relation to introduce a slow-wave branch that enables subwavelength focusing.
result: Numerical simulations and experimental demonstrations show virtual pixels far more localized than on an unmodified plate, with a tenfold reduction in pixel area and perceptually localized single- and multi-point tactile feedback.
conclusion: The method enables high-resolution haptic displays with few actuators, with potential applications in virtual reality, robotics, and human-computer interaction.

result: Valley polarization can emerge from many-body hexciton states even in the absence of coherence, indicating a new mechanism for valley control.
conclusion: The findings reveal a novel many-body contribution to valley physics, with implications for valleytronics and quantum information in TMDs.

method: The authors use differentiable resistor networks governed by Kirchhoff's laws as a physical learning platform, training them sequentially on multiple tasks and measuring forgetting.
result: They find that resistor networks exhibit catastrophic forgetting similar to neural networks, but the degree depends on task similarity and network size.
conclusion: Physical learning systems face similar challenges as digital neural networks in sequential learning, suggesting that techniques to mitigate forgetting may be needed for physical implementations.

conclusion: Provides a complete analytic solution for an extended Ising model, which may be useful for testing numerical methods and understanding phase transitions.

conclusion: The method offers a scalable approach for excited-state preparation, with potential applications in quantum simulation and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms.

title: Algorithmic Aspects Of Gauged Gaussian Fermionic Projected Entangled Pair States: Gauge Fixing And Translation Invariance
authors: Itay Gomelski, Jonathan Elyovich, Ariel Kelman, Erez Zohar, And Patrick Emonts
abstract:

Lattice gauge theories (LGTs) provide a powerful framework for studying nonperturbative phenomena in gauge theories. However, conventional approaches such as Monte Carlo (MC) simulations in imaginary time are limited, as they do not allow real-time evolution and suffer from a sign problem in many im…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023240] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops algorithmic techniques for gauge fixing and enforcing translation invariance in gauged Gaussian fermionic projected entangled pair states (PEPS), advancing tensor network methods for lattice gauge theories.
motivation: Lattice gauge theories are important for nonperturbative physics, but conventional Monte Carlo methods suffer from sign problems and cannot handle real-time evolution. Tensor network methods like PEPS offer an alternative, but gauged fermionic PEPS require careful handling of gauge redundancy and symmetries.
method: The authors propose algorithmic procedures for gauge fixing in Gaussian fermionic PEPS with gauge symmetries, and for imposing translation invariance to reduce computational cost. They likely use matrix product state techniques and variational optimization.
result: The paper presents efficient gauge-fixing algorithms and demonstrates how to enforce translation invariance, enabling more scalable simulations of lattice gauge theories with fermionic matter.
conclusion: These algorithmic advances make gauged fermionic PEPS a more practical tool for studying lattice gauge theories, potentially enabling simulations of real-time dynamics and systems with sign problems.

abstract:

The interplay of twist and strain in bilayer graphene enables the formation of moiré patterns and narrow bands that host correlated and topological phases. [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023225] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the interplay of twist and strain in bilayer graphene to engineer moiré patterns and narrow bands for correlated and topological phases.
motivation: To understand how strain, as an additional control knob, can modify the electronic properties of twisted bilayer graphene beyond the magic-angle condition.
method: Theoretical modeling and band structure calculations for strained and twisted bilayer graphene.
result: Strain can induce or modify moiré patterns and narrow bands, potentially hosting correlated and topological phases.
conclusion: Strain provides a realistic tuning parameter for band engineering in bilayer graphene, complementing twist angle control.

title: Evolving Disorder In non-Hermitian Lattices
authors: I. Komis, E. T. Kokkinakis, K. G. Makris, And E. N. Economou
abstract:

The impact of disorder on wave transport has been extensively studied in Hermitian systems, where static randomness gives rise to Anderson localization. In non-Hermitian lattices, static disorder can lead to peculiar transport features, including jumpy wave evolution. In contrast, much less is known…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023227] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the impact of evolving disorder on wave transport in non-Hermitian lattices, revealing unique transport features distinct from static disorder.
motivation: While static disorder in non-Hermitian systems has been studied, the effects of time-varying (evolving) disorder remain largely unexplored, motivating this work.
method: The authors theoretically analyze wave propagation in non-Hermitian lattices with disorder that evolves in time, using analytical and numerical methods.
result: Evolving disorder leads to peculiar transport phenomena such as jumpy wave evolution and can suppress or enhance localization depending on the disorder dynamics.
conclusion: The findings extend the understanding of disorder in non-Hermitian systems and may have implications for controlling wave transport in open systems.

title: Spinor Pairing Order Enforced By Berry Phase
authors: Yi Li And Grayson R. Frazier
abstract:

Pairing between Fermi surfaces with unequal Chern-number parity is shown to produce an exotic superconducting state characterized by half-integer monopole harmonics and a spinor-valued order parameter. Consequences include a single Bogoliubov-Weyl node that “violates” the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem, protected gapless surface states, and a fractional Mermin-Ho relation for the superfluid velocity.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022037] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper discovers a novel superconducting state with spinor order parameter and half-integer monopole harmonics arising from pairing between Fermi surfaces of unequal Chern-number parity.
motivation: To explore exotic superconducting phases that emerge from topological band structures, specifically pairing between bands with different Chern numbers.
method: Theoretical analysis using topological band theory and Berry phase concepts to construct the pairing order parameter and derive its consequences.
result: The pairing leads to a single Bogoliubov-Weyl node violating the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem, protected gapless surface states, and a fractional Mermin-Ho relation for superfluid velocity.
conclusion: This work reveals a new class of topological superconductivity with potential implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing and understanding of topological matter.

title: Taxonomy Of Prediction
authors: Alexandra Jurgens And James P. Crutchfield
abstract:
Author(s): Alexandra Jurgens and James P. Crutchfield

A prediction makes a claim about a system's future given knowledge of its past. A retrodiction makes a claim about its past given knowledge of its future. The bidirectional machine is an ambidextrous hidden Markov chain that does both optimally by making explicit in its state structure all statistic…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023218] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: The paper introduces the bidirectional machine, a hidden Markov model that optimally performs both prediction and retrodiction by encoding all statistical dependencies in its state structure.
motivation: To develop a unified framework for optimal prediction and retrodiction in stochastic processes, addressing the asymmetry between forward and backward inference.
method: The authors construct a bidirectional hidden Markov chain that captures both predictive and retrodictive information, leveraging computational mechanics and information theory.
result: The bidirectional machine achieves optimal performance for both prediction and retrodiction, revealing the minimal state complexity required for bidirectional inference.
conclusion: This work provides a foundation for understanding temporal inference in complex systems, with potential applications in time series analysis and machine learning.

title: Symmetry And Self-bound Droplets In Dipolar Molecular Gases

abstract:

Recent experiments with degenerate molecular gases dressed by elliptically polarized microwave fields have enabled new control of dipolar interactions via engineered anisotropy. [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023219] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper reveals a symmetry structure in dipolar interactions of molecular gases that leads to degeneracies among interaction parameters, enabling self-bound droplets.
motivation: To understand and control dipolar interactions in degenerate molecular gases using elliptically polarized microwave fields, which can lead to new quantum phases.
method: Theoretical analysis of the dipolar interaction symmetry under elliptical polarization, identifying degeneracies and their consequences for droplet formation.
result: Discovery of a symmetry that generates degeneracies among interaction parameters, allowing for self-bound droplet states in dipolar molecular gases.
conclusion: The findings provide a framework for engineering anisotropic dipolar interactions and may enable new quantum droplet phenomena, with implications for ultracold quantum gases.

method: The authors use theoretical modeling and simulations of electron transport in a two-terminal single-molecule junction setup.
result: The paper likely demonstrates that organic open-shell molecules can host strongly correlated phenomena, such as Kondo effects or Coulomb blockade, in transport measurements.

title: Generalized Li-Haldane Correspondence In Critical Free-fermion Systems
authors: Yuxuan Guo, Sheng Yang, And Xue-Jia Yu

Topological phenomena in quantum critical systems have recently attracted growing attention, as they go beyond the traditional paradigms of condensed matter and statistical physics. tldr: This paper generalizes the Li-Haldane correspondence to critical free-fermion systems, revealing topological edge modes in quantum critical phases.
motivation: To extend the Li-Haldane correspondence, originally for integer quantum Hall states, to critical free-fermion systems and higher dimensions, beyond traditional topological paradigms.
method: Analytical and numerical study of free-fermion models with criticality, using entanglement spectrum and edge state analysis to establish correspondence.
result: Demonstrated that critical free-fermion systems can host topological edge modes characterized by the entanglement spectrum, generalizing the Li-Haldane correspondence.
conclusion: Provides a framework for identifying topological phenomena in quantum critical systems, with implications for condensed matter and statistical physics.

result: The algorithm achieves a polynomial speedup over classical methods for certain graph families, though the exact complexity depends on graph properties.

result: A complete stochastic calculus that unifies diffusion and jump dynamics, enabling consistent treatment of pathwise observables across both regimes.
conclusion: Provides a foundational tool for stochastic processes, with potential applications in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics and beyond.

result: Contrary to expectations, significant residual scattering was observed, attributed to radiative loss mechanisms.

result: Key findings include a quantitative measure of how interactions affect the protection and spatial extent of Majorana bound states, impacting their suitability for braiding.
conclusion: The work provides a framework to evaluate realistic Majorana systems, guiding experimental efforts toward non-Abelian braiding.

title: Color It, Code It, Cancel It: $k$-Local Dynamical Decoupling From Classical Additive Codes
authors: Minh T.P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, And Stefano Bosco
abstract:
Author(s): Minh T.P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, and Stefano Bosco

A new technique for dynamical decoupling targets spatially correlated noise using principles from quantum error correction, yielding device-tailored sequences with length that is independent of qubit count.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020338] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: The paper presents a dynamical decoupling technique using classical additive codes to suppress spatially correlated noise, with sequence length independent of qubit count.
motivation: To develop efficient dynamical decoupling sequences that can handle spatially correlated noise without scaling with system size.
method: The authors map the problem of designing decoupling sequences to classical additive codes, enabling cancellation of k-local noise terms.
result: They achieve device-tailored sequences with length independent of qubit count, effectively suppressing correlated noise.
conclusion: This work bridges quantum error correction and dynamical decoupling, offering practical noise mitigation for quantum devices.

title: Abelian State Hidden Subgroup Problem: Learning Stabilizer Groups And Beyond
authors: Marcel Hinsche, Jens Eisert, And Jose Carrasco
abstract:
Author(s): Marcel Hinsche, Jens Eisert, and Jose Carrasco

An efficient quantum algorithm solves the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem, unifying key symmetry-learning primitives.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020337] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents an efficient quantum algorithm for the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem, unifying symmetry-learning primitives.
motivation: To develop a unified quantum algorithm for learning stabilizer groups and other Abelian hidden subgroup structures, which are fundamental in quantum information theory.
method: The authors propose a quantum algorithm that leverages Fourier sampling and group-theoretic techniques to solve the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem efficiently.
result: The algorithm provides an efficient solution for learning stabilizer groups and related structures, with implications for quantum error correction and symmetry learning.
conclusion: The work advances quantum algorithm design for group-theoretic problems, but its direct applications to the user's interests in thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid systems are limited.

title: String-Breaking Dynamics In Quantum Adiabatic And Diabatic Processes
authors: Federica Maria Surace, Alessio Lerose, Or Katz, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Alexander Schuckert, de Luo, Arinjoy De, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate Collins, Christopher Monroe, Zohreh Davoudi, And Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract:
Author(s): Federica Maria Surace, Alessio Lerose, Or Katz, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Alexander Schuckert, De Luo, Arinjoy De, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate Collins, Christopher Monroe, Zohreh Davoudi, and Alexey V. Gorshkov

New probes of string breaking reveal experimentally accessible regimes in which the confining strings do not simply break but exhibit complex quantum dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020331] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies string-breaking dynamics in quantum adiabatic and diabatic processes, focusing on confinement in lattice gauge theories.
motivation: To understand the real-time dynamics of string breaking in confining gauge theories, which is relevant for quantum simulation of high-energy physics.
method: The authors use a trapped-ion quantum simulator to emulate a spin chain with long-range interactions that mimic confinement, and they probe both adiabatic and diabatic quenches.
result: They observe regimes where strings do not simply break but exhibit complex quantum dynamics, including multi-string states and non-equilibrium behavior.
conclusion: The work provides new experimental probes of string breaking and demonstrates the capability of quantum simulators to study non-equilibrium phenomena in gauge theories.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols
authors: Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, And Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Author(s): Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, and Isaac H. Kim

Classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols is made scalable and efficient via propagating errors to the end of the circuit.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020329] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient classical simulation method for logical magic state preparation protocols by propagating errors to the end of the circuit.
motivation: Magic state preparation is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating these protocols is computationally expensive. The authors aim to make such simulations scalable and efficient.
method: They develop a technique that propagates errors through the circuit to the final measurement, reducing the complexity of classical simulation of logical magic state preparation.
result: The method enables efficient classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols, significantly reducing computational resources.
conclusion: This work advances the practical simulation of fault-tolerant quantum circuits, potentially aiding in the design and verification of quantum error correction protocols.

title: Abelian Multi-Cycle Codes For Single-Shot Error Correction
authors: Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, And Leonid P. Pryadko
abstract:
Author(s): Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, and Leonid P. Pryadko

A new family of quantum low-density parity-check codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, achieves single-shot fault tolerance and an approximately 1.1% pseudothreshold with significantly shorter block lengths.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020326] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a new family of quantum LDPC codes that achieve single-shot fault tolerance with shorter block lengths and a pseudothreshold of about 1.1%.
